tagline: Heart of South America, two languages strong
overview:
Paraguay lies landlocked in the middle of South America, sharing borders with Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia. The Paraguay River splits the country in two: a green, populated east of hills, farms and forest, and a vast, thorny, thinly settled west called the Chaco. The whole country is about the size of California.

About 7 million people live here, and Paraguay is unusual in that most of them speak two languages every day. Guaraní, an Indigenous language, is official alongside Spanish, and people switch between them mid-sentence. Asunción, the capital, sits on the riverbank and is one of the oldest cities in South America.

Paraguay is a presidential republic. Soybeans, beef and hydroelectric power drive its economy; the Itaipú dam it shares with Brazil is among the largest power stations in the world, and Paraguay produces far more electricity than it uses.
landAndNature: Eastern Paraguay is rolling, red-soiled and warm, with remnants of the Atlantic Forest and the Paraná River thundering along the Brazilian border. West of the river spreads the Gran Chaco, a flat expanse of thorn scrub, palm savanna and seasonal marsh that floods in the wet season and bakes hard in the dry; summer temperatures there can top 45°C, among the hottest in South America. The Pantanal's southern fringe reaches the northeast. Wildlife includes jaguars, giant anteaters, maned wolves with stilt-like legs, capybaras and the Chacoan peccary, a pig-like animal known only from fossils until living ones were found in 1975. Flocks of parrots and the enormous jabiru stork are common sights.
peopleAndCulture: Most Paraguayans are mestizo, of mixed Guaraní and Spanish descent, and Guaraní words color the way Spanish is spoken here. Tereré, cold yerba mate infused with herbs and drunk through a metal straw from a shared cup, is sipped all day in the heat and is a social ritual as much as a drink. Chipa, a chewy cheese bread made with cassava starch, is sold at bus windows, and sopa paraguaya, confusingly, is a dense corn-and-cheese cake rather than a soup. Ñandutí lace, named for the Guaraní word for spiderweb, is embroidered in fine radiating circles. The Paraguayan harp, with 36 strings and a bright, rippling sound, is the national instrument, and soccer is the national sport.
history: Guaraní peoples farmed and fished along the rivers long before Spaniards founded Asunción in 1537. Jesuit missionaries built self-governing Guaraní towns, the reducciones, in the 1600s and 1700s, whose stone ruins still stand, until Spain expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay declared independence in 1811. The War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay from 1864 to 1870 was catastrophic: Paraguay lost territory and, by many estimates, more than half its population, including most of its adult men. The Chaco War with Bolivia in the 1930s won it more territory at great cost. General Alfredo Stroessner ruled as dictator for 35 years, from 1954 to 1989, jailing and exiling opponents, until he was overthrown and democracy returned.
funFacts: Paraguay is one of very few countries where an Indigenous language, Guaraní, is spoken by most of the population, including non-Indigenous people.
The Itaipú dam on the Paraná River supplies almost all of Paraguay's electricity and a large share of Brazil's.
Paraguayans drink tereré, ice-cold mate, from a shared cup, and offering it to someone is a mark of friendship.
The Chacoan peccary was known only from fossils until scientists found living herds in the Paraguayan Chaco in 1975.
Paraguay's flag is one of the few in the world with a different emblem on each side.
